# Global association {#sec-global-association}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

library(rebook)
chapterPreamble()
```

The first step in multi-omic integration is exploratory: do the tables
associate at all? Global association methods compare the overall variation
in one table to that in another, without looking at individual features.
If no global association is found, it might not be worth to dig deeper into
feature-level associations.

This chapter gives examples of three common approaches: the Mantel
test, Procrustes analysis, and MiRKAT.

## Data

As an example dataset, we use the data from the @Hintikka2021 publication:
Xylo-Oligosaccharides in prevention of hepatic
steatosis and adipose tissue inflammation: associating taxonomic and
metabolomic patterns in fecal microbiota with biclustering.
In this study, mice were fed either with a high-fat or a low-fat diet,
and with or without prebiotics, for the purpose of studying whether prebiotics
attenuate the negative impact of a high-fat diet on health.

This example data can be loaded from the
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")` package. The data is
already in `MAE` format which is tailored for multi-assay analyses
(see [@sec-containers]). The dataset includes three different experiments:
microbial abundance data, metabolite concentrations, and data about
different biomarkers.

```{r}
#| label: global_load

library(mia)

# Load the data
data("HintikkaXOData", package = "mia")
mae <- HintikkaXOData
```

```{r}
#| label: global_experiments

# Available alternative experiments
experiments(mae)
```

```{r}
#| label: global_microbiota

# Microbiome data
getWithColData(mae, "microbiota")
```

```{r}
#| label: global_metabolites

# Metabolite data
getWithColData(mae, "metabolites")
```

```{r}
#| label: global_biomarkers

# Biomarker data
getWithColData(mae, "biomarkers")
```

Before the analysis, we preprocess both tables. The microbiome data is
agglomerated to genus level and transformed to relative abundances. For the
metabolites, we drop features with missing values, apply a log10
transformation, and standardize each metabolite.

```{r}
#| label: global_preprocess

# Microbiome
mae[["microbiota"]] <- agglomerateByRank(mae[["microbiota"]], rank = "Genus")
mae[["microbiota"]] <- transformAssay(
    mae[["microbiota"]],
    method = "relabundance"
)

# Metabolites
tse <- mae[["metabolites"]]
tse <- tse[rowSums(is.na(assay(tse, "nmr"))) == 0, ]
tse <- transformAssay(tse, assay.type = "nmr", method = "log10")
tse <- transformAssay(
    tse,
    assay.type = "log10", method = "standardize", MARGIN = "rows"
)
mae[["metabolites"]] <- tse
```

All three methods operate on sample-by-sample distances, so we calculate a
dissimilarity matrix for each table: Bray-Curtis for the microbiome and
Euclidean for the metabolites. The samples are in the same order in both
tables.

```{r}
#| label: global_dist

library(vegan)

mat_mb <- t(assay(mae[["microbiota"]], "relabundance"))
mat_mt <- t(assay(mae[["metabolites"]], "standardize"))

dist_mb <- vegdist(mat_mb, method = "bray")
dist_mt <- vegdist(mat_mt, method = "euclidean")
```

## Mantel test {#sec-mantel}

The Mantel test [@Mantel1967] correlates two distance matrices. If samples
that are similar in microbiome composition are also similar in metabolite
profiles, the correlation is positive. Significance is assessed with
permutations.

```{r}
#| label: global_mantel

set.seed(123)
mantel(dist_mb, dist_mt, method = "spearman", permutations = 999)
```

## Procrustes analysis {#sec-procrustes}

Procrustes analysis rotates, scales, and reflects one ordination to match
another as closely as possible. The permutation-based PROTEST
[@PeresNeto2001] then tests whether the two ordinations agree more than
expected by chance. Here, we compare the first two axes of principal
coordinate analysis (PCoA) of each table.

```{r}
#| label: global_procrustes

pcoa_mb <- cmdscale(dist_mb, k = 2)
pcoa_mt <- cmdscale(dist_mt, k = 2)

set.seed(123)
res <- protest(pcoa_mb, pcoa_mt, permutations = 999)
res
```

The result can be visualized by plotting how much each sample shifts between
the two ordinations.

```{r}
#| label: global_procrustes_plot

plot(res)
```

## MiRKAT {#sec-mirkat}

MiRKAT is a kernel-based framework for testing associations between
microbiome profiles and outcomes [@Zhao2015]. Its kernel RV (KRV) test
[@Zhan2017] assesses the association between the microbiome and a
multivariate outcome, such as a metabolite table.

```{r}
#| label: global_mirkat

library(MiRKAT)

kernel_mb <- D2K(as.matrix(dist_mb))
KRV(kernels.otu = kernel_mb, y = mat_mt, kernel.y = "linear")
```

The original MiRKAT test takes a single outcome. By running it separately
for each metabolite, we can see which metabolites are associated with the
overall microbiome composition. Because we perform multiple tests, the
p-values are adjusted for multiple testing.

```{r}
#| label: global_mirkat_per_metabolite

pvals <- apply(mat_mt, 2, function(y) {
    MiRKAT(y = y, Ks = kernel_mb, out_type = "C", method = "davies")[["p_values"]]
})
padj <- p.adjust(pvals, method = "fdr")

res <- data.frame(p = pvals, p_adj = padj)
res <- res[order(res[["p_adj"]]), ]
res
```

The next chapters investigate the associations between the omic layers in
more detail.
